screens.title: SELinux and AppArmor: Policy Enforcement
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we study Mandatory Access Control, using SELinux and AppArmor to enforce system-wide security policies that even the root user cannot bypass. You will learn what MAC does differently from traditional file permissions, how SELinux uses labels to control interactions, and how AppArmor confines programs by path. We will walk through reading and correcting contexts, diagnosing AVC denials, and creating targeted policy modules so your applications can run securely. You’ll also practice using booleans and port labels to enable common services like Apache acting as a reverse proxy. Importantly, the lesson shows the troubleshooting workflow: observe a denial, gather audit evidence, decide whether relabeling or a small policy module is appropriate, and apply the change without disabling policy enforcement. By the end, you should be able to interpret selinux contexts, use audit2allow responsibly, and choose the right approach when a service is blocked. Think about a service you maintain: what minimal change would you try first when it’s denied access?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives orient practical skills and understanding. First, you will understand Mandatory Access Control and how it changes the security model compared to traditional discretionary permissions. Knowing the difference helps you design systems that limit escalation risks. Second, you will administer and troubleshoot SELinux policies: read contexts, interpret AVC denials, and know when to relabel files versus creating a policy module. This skill reduces downtime by guiding targeted fixes. Third, you will generate custom SELinux policy modules using audit2allow and semodule to allow specific application behaviors without turning off enforcement. That lets you keep the protection layer active while enabling required features. Fourth, you will compare SELinux and AppArmor and choose the right tool for your distribution and operational needs. Each objective is practical: for example, when a web app is denied access, you’ll determine whether semanage fcontext and restorecon or a small module is the least-risk fix. These competencies link diagnostics to safe corrective actions and ensure production systems remain hardened.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives emphasize hands-on workflows you will perform with confidence. You will learn the workflow for diagnosing SELinux denials: check service status with sestatus, inspect file and process labels with ls -Z and ps -Z, then consult audit logs to capture the AVC denial. You will practice deciding between relabeling files and writing a minimal policy module. Relabeling with semanage fcontext and restorecon is the permanent fix for files placed into managed directories. Writing a policy module via audit2allow and semodule is appropriate when a service legitimately needs a behavior not covered by existing types. You will also practice toggling booleans, for example using setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on to permit Apache network connections. Finally, you will learn AppArmor basics so you can operate in distributions that use path-based profiles, using aa-status, aa-complain, aa-enforce, and aa-genprof to build profiles. Each practical skill reduces the temptation to disable policy and keeps systems harder to exploit.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Practical Skills
Commands to Know
sestatus • ls -Z • ps -Z • semanage • restorecon • chcon • audit2allow • semodule
Practice the flow: verify mode, inspect contexts, reproduce denial, collect audit evidence, choose relabel or module.
Decision Guide
  • Files in managed directories: use semanage fcontext + restorecon.
  • Missing policy for an expected behavior: use audit2allow to propose a module.
  • Avoid chcon for permanent fixes; it’s temporary.
Quick Tip
Use permissive mode locally to collect denials before applying changes in enforcing production systems. Permissive lets you see what would be blocked without service interruption.
Why This Matters

screens.title: MAC vs DAC — Why Labels and Profiles Matter
screens.narratorSegment: Mandatory Access Control, or MAC, is a security model where the kernel enforces system-wide policies that determine which subjects can access which objects. Unlike DAC, which relies on file ownership and discretionary permission changes, MAC does not allow individual users or services to grant broad permissions on their own. That matters because it prevents a compromised user or poorly written application from granting itself or others access beyond its confinement. A concrete example is a web server process: under DAC it runs with the privileges of its user and file permissions determine access; under MAC, the web server is bound to a label such as httpd_t, and files labeled httpd_sys_content_t define what that process can read. If an attacker gains control of the web process, MAC limits what the process can do based on policy, reducing lateral movement. A common misconception is that MAC is an all-or-nothing lockdown. In practice, MAC is flexible: SELinux provides booleans to toggle permitted behaviors and policy modules to extend capabilities carefully. The core takeaway is this: MAC shifts enforcement from user discretion to centrally managed labels or profiles, which makes systemic security more robust. Consider: when would you prefer relabeling a directory over creating a new policy module?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: MAC enforces system-wide rules at the kernel level so policy, not user choice, governs access decisions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › MAC vs DAC
Definition

Mandatory Access Control

Kernel-enforced policy binds subjects and objects using labels or profiles so that access cannot be bypassed by users or processes.

Key points:
  • SELinux: label-based contexts for files, processes, and ports.
  • AppArmor: path-based profiles tied to executables.
  • MAC persists across user privilege changes.
Key Takeaway

Use MAC to reduce the damage possible from a compromised process; prefer policy changes over disabling enforcement.

Analogy & Example
Think of DAC as personal keys each user controls and MAC as a central access policy controlled by the building manager. If one tenant is compromised, they cannot rekey the building under MAC.
Concrete Example
# File under wrong context will be denied
ls -Z /var/www/html/index.html
# process context for Apache
ps -Z | grep httpd
Label-based: httpd_t and httpd_sys_content_t
Path-based: AppArmor profiles in /etc/apparmor.d/

screens.title: SELinux Security Contexts
screens.narratorSegment: SELinux attaches a security context to objects and processes. A context follows the form user:role:type:level. In practice, the type field drives most enforcement decisions: types like httpd_t denote process domains, while types like httpd_sys_content_t denote file content types. When a process labeled httpd_t tries to access a file labeled httpd_sys_content_t, the policy determines whether that interaction is allowed. For troubleshooting, you will read contexts with ls -Z for files and ps -Z for processes. Use chcon to make a temporary change, and semanage fcontext combined with restorecon to set a permanent default. A common trap is moving files into an SELinux-managed directory without relabeling them; the displayed permissions may look correct under DAC, but SELinux can still deny access because types don’t match. A practical example: you put web content into /srv/webapp/html and see a 403. After ls -Z shows default_t, you run semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/webapp/html(/.*)?" and then restorecon -Rv /srv/webapp/html to apply the correct labels. The core insight is: types map behavior; ensure files and processes carry compatible types. SELinux Security Contexts means a context like user:role:type:level defines security attributes. the type is the primary enforcement key between processes and objects.. In practical terms, user:role:type:level and why the type matters most. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › SELinux Contexts
Context Structure
A context is four parts: user, role, type, and level. Commands show these labels for inspection and action.
# View file context
ls -Z /srv/webapp/html/index.html
# View process context
ps -Z | grep httpd
# Temporarily change context
sudo chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/webapp/html/index.html
Key Takeaway

Always verify types for both the process and the resource; mismatched types are the most common cause of denials.

Permanent Labeling
Use semanage fcontext to define defaults and restorecon to apply them.
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/webapp/html(/.*)?"
sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/webapp/html
Misconception: chcon is permanent. It is temporary and can be reset by restorecon or relabel operations. For lasting changes, use semanage fcontext.

screens.title: SELinux Modes and Safe Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: SELinux runs in three modes: enforcing, permissive, and disabled. Enforcing applies the policy and denies violations, permissive logs violations without blocking, and disabled turns off enforcement entirely. For production systems you want enforcing, because it provides active protection. When troubleshooting, permissive mode is a valuable tool: it lets you reproduce and collect AVC denials without disrupting service. Use sestatus to check the current mode. A safe troubleshooting workflow is to switch a non-production test host to permissive, exercise the application to produce denials, then analyze logs and craft fixes. Never use disabled as a routine fix — it removes the protection envelope. A concrete example: if Apache cannot serve files in a new directory, enable permissive on a test instance, reproduce the access attempt, run ausearch or examine /var/log/audit/audit. log, and use audit2allow to propose a module. After validating the proposed module and confirming relabeling won’t suffice, install the module and return the system to enforcing. The misconception to avoid is treating permissive as a long-term mode; it is a temporary diagnostic state. After remediation, revert to enforcing to keep protections active.

keyIdea.text: Use permissive for controlled troubleshooting, enforcing for production, and avoid disabling SELinux as a shortcut.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › SELinux Modes
Modes Explained
  • Enforcing — policy enforced and violations blocked and logged.
  • Permissive — violations logged but not blocked; for diagnostics.
  • Disabled — SELinux enforcement is off; not recommended.
Check mode: sestatus. Temporarily set permissive for debugging, then return to enforcing after fixes.
Troubleshooting Workflow
1) Reproduce denial in permissive. 2) Gather AVC entries. 3) Decide relabel or module. 4) Apply change. 5) Return to enforcing and verify.
# Check mode
sestatus
# Temporarily set permissive (appropriate for test)
sudo setenforce 0
# Return to enforcing
sudo setenforce 1
Misconception: setting permissive on production is safe — it will hide active policy violations. Use permissive only on isolated testing or short windows with clear monitoring.

screens.title: Inspecting Labels and Correcting File Contexts
screens.narratorSegment: Practical inspection begins with a few simple commands. Use ls -Z to view file contexts; the output shows the entire security context including type. Use ps -Z to show the context attached to a running process. If a file lands in a web directory with a default or incorrect type, Apache will be denied even if POSIX permissions are correct. chcon can change a file’s context immediately and is useful for quick tests, but it’s temporary and may be undone by restorecon. For a permanent fix, declare the correct default context with semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/path(/.*)?" then run restorecon -Rv to apply it recursively. A concrete step sequence: after creating content under /srv/webapp/html, run ls -Z to confirm it lacks httpd_sys_content_t. If so, add an fcontext entry, restorecon, verify with ls -Z again, and restart httpd. A common mistake is using chcon as the long-term solution. chcon may solve an immediate issue but will be reset by relabels. The right long-term approach is semanage fcontext followed by restorecon. After these steps, web content should be served without disabling SELinux.

keyIdea.text: Use ls -Z and ps -Z to inspect contexts; use semanage fcontext + restorecon for permanent labeling; chcon only for temporary tests.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Inspect & Correct Contexts
Inspection Commands
ls -Z /srv/webapp/html/index.html
ps -Z | grep httpd
Verify the type fields: the process should show httpd_t and the files httpd_sys_content_t for normal Apache serving.
Fixing Contexts
# Temporary change
sudo chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/webapp/html/index.html
# Permanent default
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/webapp/html(/.*)?"
sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/webapp/html
Example mistake: moving files into a managed directory without running restorecon will leave them with the old type and cause access denied.

screens.title: AVC Denials and Audit Logs
screens.narratorSegment: When SELinux blocks an action, the kernel records an AVC denial. These denials appear in /var/log/audit/audit. log or through journalctl and can be searched with ausearch. The denial contains the subject and object contexts and the requested operation, which is essential to determine the cause. A typical diagnostic sequence is: reproduce the failure, collect AVC messages from audit. log, and feed them into audit2allow to see a Suggested allow rule. For example, if httpd attempts network access or an unexpected file access, you will see an entry naming the process domain and the file or port type. Use ausearch -c 'httpd' --raw to filter entries for the service and then run audit2allow -M modulename to generate a. te and. pp. However, don’t immediately apply generated modules blindly — examine the suggested rules to ensure they are minimal and appropriate. A common misconception is that audit2allow always produces safe rules. It produces what would permit the observed actions; you must confirm those actions are legitimate behavior and not a sign of compromised software. Every generated module should be reviewed before installation with semodule -i.

keyIdea.text: Collect AVC denials, analyze with audit2allow, review suggested rules, and install minimal policy modules only after validation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › AVC & Audit
Locate Denials
# Search for httpd denials
sudo ausearch -c 'httpd' --raw
# Or inspect the audit log
sudo tail -n 200 /var/log/audit/audit.log
Denial entries include source and target contexts and the requested permission set; these details guide your fix.
Analyze with audit2allow
# Generate a module from recent denials
sudo ausearch -c 'httpd' --raw | audit2allow -M webapp_fix
# This produces webapp_fix.te and webapp_fix.pp
Inspect the .te file and confirm the allow rules are specific and justified before installing with semodule -i.

screens.title: Creating and Installing a Custom SELinux Module
screens.narratorSegment: When audit2allow indicates a legitimate need, you can create a minimal SELinux module. The typical commands are: extract denials, pipe them to audit2allow -M modulename to produce a modulename. te and modulename. pp, review the. te file to ensure the allow rules are narrowly scoped, then install with semodule -i modulename. pp. For example, if Apache tried to access a directory or network resource not covered by existing types, audit2allow will suggest allow lines for httpd_t against a particular target type. After reviewing and ensuring there is no broader privilege escalation, run sudo semodule -i modulename. pp to load the module into the policy. A concrete example in the lab is running ausearch -c 'httpd' --raw | audit2allow -M webapp_content_fix resulting in webapp_content_fix. te and webapp_content_fix. pp. Inspect the. te to confirm it only permits the observed operations, and then semodule -i webapp_content_fix. pp. Remember that modules should be minimal; if the behavior is common and aligns with a known type, prefer correct labeling with semanage fcontext rather than adding broad allow rules. After module installation, verify the service functions and that AVC denials for that action cease.

keyIdea.title: Module Workflow
keyIdea.text: Generate a suggested module with audit2allow, review the .te for minimality, and install the compiled .pp with semodule -i if justified.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Policy Module
Generate Module
sudo ausearch -c 'httpd' --raw | audit2allow -M webapp_content_fix
# Produces webapp_content_fix.te and webapp_content_fix.pp
Review the .te file in a pager and ensure each allow rule is justified for the expected behavior only.
Install & Verify
# Install the compiled module
sudo semodule -i webapp_content_fix.pp
# Confirm change and test service
sudo systemctl restart httpd
If the installed rules are too broad, remove the module with semodule -r and refine the policy or prefer relabeling instead.

screens.title: Booleans and Ports: Enabling Common Behaviors
screens.narratorSegment: SELinux exposes configurable toggles called booleans that enable or disable parts of the policy without recompiling. For web services, a common boolean is httpd_can_network_connect, which allows Apache to initiate outbound network connections. Use setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on to persist the change across reboots, and check booleans with getsebool -a. For ports, SELinux maps TCP/UDP ports to port types; if your service needs a nonstandard port like 8080, add it to the appropriate port type with semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080. Verify the mapping with semanage port -l | grep http_port_t. A practical scenario is configuring Apache as a reverse proxy to a backend on port 8080: you must label the port in SELinux and enable network connect capability for httpd. A common misconception is that semanage port changes are risky; they are the correct way to tell SELinux that a given port should be associated with a known type. Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Booleans & Ports
Booleans
# Make httpd network-connect allowed permanently
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
# List booleans
sudo getsebool -a
Booleans tune policy without module compilation and survive reboots when -P is used.
Port Labeling
# Add port 8080 to http_port_t
sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080
# Verify
sudo semanage port -l | grep http_port_t
Use semanage port to let services listen on nonstandard ports under existing SELinux types.

screens.title: Lab: Configure Apache to Serve /srv/webapp/html
screens.narratorSegment: This lab walks through configuring a custom web application in /srv/webapp/html and enabling Apache to serve it while SELinux remains enforcing. First, ensure SELinux is enforcing with sestatus and setenforce if needed. Install and start Apache, create /srv/webapp/html/index. html, and chown the files to the apache user. Initially, ls -Z will show a default type like default_t and Apache will be denied access. Attempt to access the page to reproduce the 403 and capture AVC denials using ausearch or by viewing /var/log/audit/audit. log. Next, define the correct file context with semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/webapp/html(/.*)?" and apply it using restorecon -Rv /srv/webapp/html. Verify with ls -Z that the file now has httpd_sys_content_t. If Apache needs to proxy to a backend on port 8080, add that port with semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 and enable network connections with setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on. Finally, restart Apache and confirm the content is served. The main lesson here is to follow diagnosis before change and prefer permanent labeling where appropriate. Lab Timeline
1. Setup and verify
Install httpd, create /srv/webapp/html/index.html, and confirm SELinux is enforcing with sestatus.

Try to access the page, then use ausearch -c 'httpd' --raw or check /var/log/audit/audit.log to gather messages.

Restart httpd, test the site, and ensure AVC denials related to the fix no longer appear.

screens.title: AppArmor Overview and Key Commands
screens.narratorSegment: AppArmor is an alternative MAC system that confines programs based on their executable path and profile rules stored in /etc/apparmor. d/. Profiles enumerate allowed file access, network, and capability operations for a program. Profiles can be in enforce mode, which blocks and logs violations, or complain mode, which only logs them — similar to SELinux’s enforcing and permissive. Use aa-status to view loaded profiles and their modes. To change a profile into complain mode for learning and profile generation, run sudo aa-complain /path/to/binary and to enforce it sudo aa-enforce /path/to/binary. Generating a new profile typically involves placing an application into complain mode, exercising it through typical workflows, and then using aa-genprof to help assemble a profile from observed accesses. AppArmor’s path-based approach can be simpler for per-application confinement on Debian and Ubuntu systems, but it provides different trade-offs compared to SELinux: labels give SELinux more system-wide, fine-grained control while AppArmor is often easier to author for individual programs. The practical takeaway is to know the tool your distribution uses and follow its complain→profile→enforce workflow to build safe confinement. AppArmor Overview and Key Commands means apparmor confines by path; use aa-complain, aa-genprof, and aa-enforce to build and activate profiles without disabling enforcement.. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › AppArmor
Core Ideas
AppArmor profiles live under /etc/apparmor.d/ and attach rules to an executable path rather than applying labels to every file and process.
# Status
sudo aa-status
# Put profile in complain
sudo aa-complain /usr/bin/myapp
# Enforce profile
sudo aa-enforce /usr/bin/myapp
Profile Generation
Typical flow: complain mode to collect logs, aa-genprof to generate a profile, review and then enforce.
Comparison note: AppArmor is often simpler for individual app rules; SELinux offers broader, label-based system policy. Choose based on distribution and operational needs.

screens.title: Choosing Between SELinux and AppArmor
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing SELinux or AppArmor depends on the distribution and your policy goals. SELinux is label-based and provides fine-grained, system-wide control: every file, process, and port can have a context, which is powerful for comprehensive containment. AppArmor is path-based and often easier to author for individual applications because profiles map to executable paths. A practical trade-off is manageability versus granularity: SELinux can be more complex to learn but scales well for system-wide policies, while AppArmor can be faster to adopt for single-app confinement. Common mistakes include: moving files into protected directories without relabeling them, applying chcon as a permanent fix, and installing audit2allow modules without reviewing their suggested rules. Another frequent error is toggling SELinux to disabled to stop denials; this removes an important defense layer. When troubleshooting, prefer permissive mode temporarily and use relabeling with semanage fcontext and restorecon if files are simply mislabeled. Reserve module generation for behavior not covered by existing types. The final question to carry forward is: what is the least-privilege change that restores functionality while preserving enforcement? When to Use SELinux
  • Require fine-grained, label-based system-wide policy.
  • Need port and resource labeling for many services.
  • Operate on distributions where SELinux is standard.
When to Use AppArmor
  • Prefer quicker per-application profile authoring.
  • Target single executables without relabeling the filesystem.
  • Work on Debian/Ubuntu where AppArmor is default.
Common Troubleshooting Checklist
1) Confirm mode with sestatus or aa-status. 2) Inspect contexts with ls -Z and ps -Z or AppArmor logs. 3) Reproduce denials in permissive/complain. 4) Decide relabel vs module/profile. 5) Apply minimal change and verify.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we study Mandatory Access Control, using SELinux and AppArmor to enforce system-wide security policies that even the root user cannot bypass. You will learn what MAC does differently from traditional file permissions, how SELinux uses labels to control interactions, and how AppArmor confines programs by path. We will walk through reading and correcting contexts, diagnosing AVC denials, and creating targeted policy modules so your applications can run securely. You’ll also practice using booleans and port labels to enable common services like Apache acting as a reverse proxy. Importantly, the lesson shows the troubleshooting workflow: observe a denial, gather audit evidence, decide whether relabeling or a small policy module is appropriate, and apply the change without disabling policy enforcement. By the end, you should be able to interpret selinux contexts, use audit2allow responsibly, and choose the right approach when a service is blocked. Think about a service you maintain: what minimal change would you try first when it’s denied access?

These learning objectives orient practical skills and understanding. First, you will understand Mandatory Access Control and how it changes the security model compared to traditional discretionary permissions. Knowing the difference helps you design systems that limit escalation risks. Second, you will administer and troubleshoot SELinux policies: read contexts, interpret AVC denials, and know when to relabel files versus creating a policy module. This skill reduces downtime by guiding targeted fixes. Third, you will generate custom SELinux policy modules using audit2allow and semodule to allow specific application behaviors without turning off enforcement. That lets you keep the protection layer active while enabling required features. Fourth, you will compare SELinux and AppArmor and choose the right tool for your distribution and operational needs. Each objective is practical: for example, when a web app is denied access, you’ll determine whether semanage fcontext and restorecon or a small module is the least-risk fix. These competencies link diagnostics to safe corrective actions and ensure production systems remain hardened.

These objectives emphasize hands-on workflows you will perform with confidence. You will learn the workflow for diagnosing SELinux denials: check service status with sestatus, inspect file and process labels with ls -Z and ps -Z, then consult audit logs to capture the AVC denial. You will practice deciding between relabeling files and writing a minimal policy module. Relabeling with semanage fcontext and restorecon is the permanent fix for files placed into managed directories. Writing a policy module via audit2allow and semodule is appropriate when a service legitimately needs a behavior not covered by existing types. You will also practice toggling booleans, for example using setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on to permit Apache network connections. Finally, you will learn AppArmor basics so you can operate in distributions that use path-based profiles, using aa-status, aa-complain, aa-enforce, and aa-genprof to build profiles. Each practical skill reduces the temptation to disable policy and keeps systems harder to exploit.

Mandatory Access Control, or MAC, is a security model where the kernel enforces system-wide policies that determine which subjects can access which objects. Unlike DAC, which relies on file ownership and discretionary permission changes, MAC does not allow individual users or services to grant broad permissions on their own. That matters because it prevents a compromised user or poorly written application from granting itself or others access beyond its confinement. A concrete example is a web server process: under DAC it runs with the privileges of its user and file permissions determine access; under MAC, the web server is bound to a label such as httpd_t, and files labeled httpd_sys_content_t define what that process can read. If an attacker gains control of the web process, MAC limits what the process can do based on policy, reducing lateral movement. A common misconception is that MAC is an all-or-nothing lockdown. In practice, MAC is flexible: SELinux provides booleans to toggle permitted behaviors and policy modules to extend capabilities carefully. The core takeaway is this: MAC shifts enforcement from user discretion to centrally managed labels or profiles, which makes systemic security more robust. Consider: when would you prefer relabeling a directory over creating a new policy module?

SELinux attaches a security context to objects and processes. A context follows the form user:role:type:level. In practice, the type field drives most enforcement decisions: types like httpd_t denote process domains, while types like httpd_sys_content_t denote file content types. When a process labeled httpd_t tries to access a file labeled httpd_sys_content_t, the policy determines whether that interaction is allowed. For troubleshooting, you will read contexts with ls -Z for files and ps -Z for processes. Use chcon to make a temporary change, and semanage fcontext combined with restorecon to set a permanent default. A common trap is moving files into an SELinux-managed directory without relabeling them; the displayed permissions may look correct under DAC, but SELinux can still deny access because types don’t match. A practical example: you put web content into /srv/webapp/html and see a 403. After ls -Z shows default_t, you run semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/webapp/html(/.*)?" and then restorecon -Rv /srv/webapp/html to apply the correct labels. The core insight is: types map behavior; ensure files and processes carry compatible types. SELinux Security Contexts means a context like user:role:type:level defines security attributes. the type is the primary enforcement key between processes and objects.. In practical terms, user:role:type:level and why the type matters most. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SELinux runs in three modes: enforcing, permissive, and disabled. Enforcing applies the policy and denies violations, permissive logs violations without blocking, and disabled turns off enforcement entirely. For production systems you want enforcing, because it provides active protection. When troubleshooting, permissive mode is a valuable tool: it lets you reproduce and collect AVC denials without disrupting service. Use sestatus to check the current mode. A safe troubleshooting workflow is to switch a non-production test host to permissive, exercise the application to produce denials, then analyze logs and craft fixes. Never use disabled as a routine fix — it removes the protection envelope. A concrete example: if Apache cannot serve files in a new directory, enable permissive on a test instance, reproduce the access attempt, run ausearch or examine /var/log/audit/audit. log, and use audit2allow to propose a module. After validating the proposed module and confirming relabeling won’t suffice, install the module and return the system to enforcing. The misconception to avoid is treating permissive as a long-term mode; it is a temporary diagnostic state. After remediation, revert to enforcing to keep protections active.

Practical inspection begins with a few simple commands. Use ls -Z to view file contexts; the output shows the entire security context including type. Use ps -Z to show the context attached to a running process. If a file lands in a web directory with a default or incorrect type, Apache will be denied even if POSIX permissions are correct. chcon can change a file’s context immediately and is useful for quick tests, but it’s temporary and may be undone by restorecon. For a permanent fix, declare the correct default context with semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/path(/.*)?" then run restorecon -Rv to apply it recursively. A concrete step sequence: after creating content under /srv/webapp/html, run ls -Z to confirm it lacks httpd_sys_content_t. If so, add an fcontext entry, restorecon, verify with ls -Z again, and restart httpd. A common mistake is using chcon as the long-term solution. chcon may solve an immediate issue but will be reset by relabels. The right long-term approach is semanage fcontext followed by restorecon. After these steps, web content should be served without disabling SELinux.

When SELinux blocks an action, the kernel records an AVC denial. These denials appear in /var/log/audit/audit. log or through journalctl and can be searched with ausearch. The denial contains the subject and object contexts and the requested operation, which is essential to determine the cause. A typical diagnostic sequence is: reproduce the failure, collect AVC messages from audit. log, and feed them into audit2allow to see a Suggested allow rule. For example, if httpd attempts network access or an unexpected file access, you will see an entry naming the process domain and the file or port type. Use ausearch -c 'httpd' --raw to filter entries for the service and then run audit2allow -M modulename to generate a. te and. pp. However, don’t immediately apply generated modules blindly — examine the suggested rules to ensure they are minimal and appropriate. A common misconception is that audit2allow always produces safe rules. It produces what would permit the observed actions; you must confirm those actions are legitimate behavior and not a sign of compromised software. Every generated module should be reviewed before installation with semodule -i.

When audit2allow indicates a legitimate need, you can create a minimal SELinux module. The typical commands are: extract denials, pipe them to audit2allow -M modulename to produce a modulename. te and modulename. pp, review the. te file to ensure the allow rules are narrowly scoped, then install with semodule -i modulename. pp. For example, if Apache tried to access a directory or network resource not covered by existing types, audit2allow will suggest allow lines for httpd_t against a particular target type. After reviewing and ensuring there is no broader privilege escalation, run sudo semodule -i modulename. pp to load the module into the policy. A concrete example in the lab is running ausearch -c 'httpd' --raw | audit2allow -M webapp_content_fix resulting in webapp_content_fix. te and webapp_content_fix. pp. Inspect the. te to confirm it only permits the observed operations, and then semodule -i webapp_content_fix. pp. Remember that modules should be minimal; if the behavior is common and aligns with a known type, prefer correct labeling with semanage fcontext rather than adding broad allow rules. After module installation, verify the service functions and that AVC denials for that action cease.

SELinux exposes configurable toggles called booleans that enable or disable parts of the policy without recompiling. For web services, a common boolean is httpd_can_network_connect, which allows Apache to initiate outbound network connections. Use setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on to persist the change across reboots, and check booleans with getsebool -a. For ports, SELinux maps TCP/UDP ports to port types; if your service needs a nonstandard port like 8080, add it to the appropriate port type with semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080. Verify the mapping with semanage port -l | grep http_port_t. A practical scenario is configuring Apache as a reverse proxy to a backend on port 8080: you must label the port in SELinux and enable network connect capability for httpd. A common misconception is that semanage port changes are risky; they are the correct way to tell SELinux that a given port should be associated with a known type. Use booleans and port labels to enable expected network behaviors while preserving enforcement for other resources. Always verify with audit logs if issues persist. Booleans and Ports: Enabling Common Behaviors means use booleans for policy toggles and semanage port to map nonstandard ports to existing types so services can bind and connect as intended.. This lab walks through configuring a custom web application in /srv/webapp/html and enabling Apache to serve it while SELinux remains enforcing. First, ensure SELinux is enforcing with sestatus and setenforce if needed. Install and start Apache, create /srv/webapp/html/index. html, and chown the files to the apache user. Initially, ls -Z will show a default type like default_t and Apache will be denied access. Attempt to access the page to reproduce the 403 and capture AVC denials using ausearch or by viewing /var/log/audit/audit. log. Next, define the correct file context with semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/webapp/html(/.*)?" and apply it using restorecon -Rv /srv/webapp/html. Verify with ls -Z that the file now has httpd_sys_content_t. If Apache needs to proxy to a backend on port 8080, add that port with semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 and enable network connections with setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on. Finally, restart Apache and confirm the content is served. The main lesson here is to follow diagnosis before change and prefer permanent labeling where appropriate. AppArmor is an alternative MAC system that confines programs based on their executable path and profile rules stored in /etc/apparmor. d/. Profiles enumerate allowed file access, network, and capability operations for a program. Profiles can be in enforce mode, which blocks and logs violations, or complain mode, which only logs them — similar to SELinux’s enforcing and permissive. Use aa-status to view loaded profiles and their modes. To change a profile into complain mode for learning and profile generation, run sudo aa-complain /path/to/binary and to enforce it sudo aa-enforce /path/to/binary. Generating a new profile typically involves placing an application into complain mode, exercising it through typical workflows, and then using aa-genprof to help assemble a profile from observed accesses. AppArmor’s path-based approach can be simpler for per-application confinement on Debian and Ubuntu systems, but it provides different trade-offs compared to SELinux: labels give SELinux more system-wide, fine-grained control while AppArmor is often easier to author for individual programs. The practical takeaway is to know the tool your distribution uses and follow its complain→profile→enforce workflow to build safe confinement. Choosing SELinux or AppArmor depends on the distribution and your policy goals. SELinux is label-based and provides fine-grained, system-wide control: every file, process, and port can have a context, which is powerful for comprehensive containment. AppArmor is path-based and often easier to author for individual applications because profiles map to executable paths. A practical trade-off is manageability versus granularity: SELinux can be more complex to learn but scales well for system-wide policies, while AppArmor can be faster to adopt for single-app confinement. Common mistakes include: moving files into protected directories without relabeling them, applying chcon as a permanent fix, and installing audit2allow modules without reviewing their suggested rules. Another frequent error is toggling SELinux to disabled to stop denials; this removes an important defense layer. When troubleshooting, prefer permissive mode temporarily and use relabeling with semanage fcontext and restorecon if files are simply mislabeled. Reserve module generation for behavior not covered by existing types. The final question to carry forward is: what is the least-privilege change that restores functionality while preserving enforcement? Choosing Between SELinux and AppArmor means select selinux for label-driven system-wide control; choose apparmor for simpler path-based per-application profiles. always prefer targeted fixes over disabling policy.. These three concise points capture the practical essence of SELinux and AppArmor policy enforcement. First, MAC shifts enforcement from users to system policy; use it to confine processes and reduce compromise impact. Second, for SELinux, contexts are central: inspect with ls -Z and ps -Z, fix with semanage fcontext and restorecon, and use chcon only for temporary tests. Third, handle denials methodically: reproduce the failure, collect AVC entries, analyze with audit2allow, review suggested rules, and apply a minimal module only if relabeling is insufficient. Keep SELinux in enforcing for production systems and use permissive or complain modes only for controlled troubleshooting. These practices let you maintain functionality without removing an important layer of defense.
